name: Saterland Frisian
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Peters, Jörg. 2019. Saterland Frisian (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 49(2): 223-230. doi:10.1017/S0025100317000226 (first published online 15 June 2017). Publisher PDF (Cambridge Core).
catalog_quote: The distribution of primary word stress in Saterland Frisian can be characterized with reference to the phonological word as defined by Wiese (2000) for Standard German. Specifically, a phonological word in Saterland Frisian can consist of one of the following: (i) a lexical stem, which may be extended by (a) prefixes with a reduced vowel, (b) the prefix /bi/, or (c) suffixes that begin with a vowel; (ii) a prefix with a full vowel (except /bi/); and (iii) a suffix that has a full vowel and begins with a consonant. Morphological words comprise one or more phonological words. In morphological words comprising a single phonological word the primary word stress falls on the last stressed syllable. If they comprise more than one phonological word, the primary word stress falls on the last stressed syllable of the first phonological word. An illustration of how stress works in Saterland Frisian complex words is given below. Phonological words are in parentheses. Stressed syllables are underlined. Note that the rules do also apply to loans like /zəˈlɔːt/ and /ˌeləˈfant/. ... /ˈtumə/ ... (tumə) ... 'thumb' / /zəˈlɔːt/ ... (zəlɔːt) ... 'salad' / /biˈprɔːljə/ bi+prɔːl+jə (biprɔːljə) 'to praise' / /ˈutˌdrIŋkə/ ut+drIŋk+ə (ut)(drIŋkə) 'to drink up' / /ˈdIskdɔu̯k/ dIsk+dɔu̯k (dIsk)(dɔu̯k) 'tablecloth' / /ˌeːləˈfant/ eːləfant (eləfant) 'elephant'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is morphologically/prosodically governed, on the German model (Peters follows Wiese 2000): a phonological word is a lexical stem plus any schwa-prefixes, the prefix bi-, and vowel-initial suffixes; full-vowel prefixes (except bi-) and consonant-initial full-vowel suffixes form their own phonological words. Within a single phonological word primary stress goes on its last stressable (full-vowel) syllable — in practice the stem, since schwa cannot bear stress (/ˈtumə/ 'thumb', /biˈprɔːljə/ 'to praise'); in loans this yields final stress (/zəˈlɔːt/ 'salad', /ˌeːləˈfant/ 'elephant'). In words of more than one phonological word (particle verbs, compounds) primary stress is on the last stressed syllable of the FIRST phonological word (/ˈutˌdrɪŋkə/ 'to drink up', /ˈdɪskdɔu̯k/ 'tablecloth'). The Sprachlehre des Saterfriesischen (Slofstra & Hoekstra 2023: 97-98) agrees for verbs: separable verb particles are stressed (AN-aaskje), inseparable prefix verbs stress the stem (be-fläkke).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated as a rule; secondary stress is marked in the examples on the non-initial phonological word of compounds (/ˈutˌdrɪŋkə/) and on the initial full-vowel syllable of loans (/ˌeːləˈfant/, ˌäärmˈzoalig, ˌstjúurˈfräi).
new_statements.exceptions: Peters (citing Fort 2015) lists compounds borrowed from Northern Standard German with stress on the second element, unlike their German cognates: Sfrs. ˌäärmˈzoalig vs. Nsg. ˈarmˌselig 'miserable', lichtˈfäidig vs. ˈleichtˌfertig 'careless', ˌstjúurˈfräi vs. ˈsteuerˌfrei 'tax-free' — explained as the loans being treated as single phonological words whose last stressed syllable attracts primary stress. Also: 'In today's language, there is no clear indication of a word accent distinction between GESTOSSENER TON ('push tone') and GESCHLIFFENER TON ('dragging tone'), as assumed by Siebs (1889) for the Saterland Frisian of his time.' Stress rules apply to loans too. Slofstra & Hoekstra note variable stress in a few prefix verbs (mis-gunge / MISS-gunge; truch-ÖILE / TRUCH-öile) and a stress-distinguished pair uur-slo 'not heed' vs UUR-slo 'get warm'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (morphological word made of one or more phonological words, incl. compounds and particle verbs); based on citation-form elicitation and recorded passage from three elderly trilingual speakers (Ramsloh, Scharrel, Strücklingen). Intonation is said to match Northern Standard German. Classification as 'morphologically determined' is my mapping: stress is stem/prosodic-word-determined, not position-counted or weight-based; 'fixed: final syllable' would fit only loans/simplex words read as 'last full-vowel syllable'.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog's sate1242 'Ems-Weser Frisian' bundles living Saterland Frisian (Ems Frisian; dialects of Ramsloh, Strücklingen, Scharrel/Sedelsberg) with the extinct Weser Frisian of Wangerooge/Wursten (Glottolog refs Ehrentraut 1849-54, Versloot 2001, Siebs 1954, Gregersen 2023 are Wangeroogic). The statement quoted is for Saterland Frisian only (Peters 2019, three speakers from Ramsloh, Scharrel, Strücklingen). Taalportaal's Saterfrisian introduction notes that Old Weser Frisian differed: 'in some words, the main accent fell on the second syllable, with reduction of the first one' (kma 'come', snu 'son'; citing Versloot 2001a,b) — so the Wangerooge variety should not be assumed to share the Saterland pattern.

tone_statements.citation: Peters, Jörg. 2008. Saterfrisian intonation: An analysis of historical recordings. Us Wurk 57: 141-169.
tone_statements.quote: The assignment of word and sentence stress in Saterfrisian (SFR) is very similar to that of High and Low German. Unusual word stress is found in some compounds and other morphologically complex forms, mostly loans from High German. [p. 149] ... We conclude that accent choice cannot be predicted from syllable structure, which leaves open the possibility that the distinction between accent 1 and accent 2 is a word accent distinction. Our corpus does not contain a tonal minimal pair [p. 162] ... Rather, we assume that accent 1 and accent 2 derive from an older word accent distinction, which is linked to Siebs' (1889) distinction between Stosston and Schleifton. The apparent absence of tonal minimal pairs, however, suggests that the functional load of this distinction in the speech of our informants is low. [p. 166]
